question.text: What is the fundamental difference in how the three underlying markets (equity, currency, bond) determine value?

answer.text: Equity value is driven by corporate earnings and growth expectations; currency value is driven by relative economic fundamentals and interest rate differentials between countries; bond value is driven by interest rates, credit quality, and maturity
All three markets determine value solely based on supply and demand with no fundamental drivers
Equity and currency values are determined by government policy while bond values are market-determined
All three markets use the same discounted cash flow model with identical inputs

explanation.text: The Logic: Each underlying market is priced off a distinct set of fundamental drivers. Equity values reflect a company's earnings, growth prospects, and dividends. Currency values reflect relative economic fundamentals between two countries — inflation, growth, trade balance, and especially interest-rate differentials. Bond values reflect prevailing interest rates, the issuer's credit quality, and time to maturity. This is why derivative pricing models also differ across asset classes. The Trap: Supply and demand affects every market but is not the only driver. Government policy and market forces both matter — none of these markets is purely government-set. And while DCF principles can apply broadly, the cash flows being discounted differ (earnings vs coupons/principal), so the inputs are not identical. Note: The NISM Series I (Currency), Series IV (Interest Rate) and Series VIII (Equity) workbook pages reviewed support pieces of this framing (relative economic factors for currencies, yield-curve/credit context for bonds, equity-market role) but do not present this exact three-way comparison of value drivers in one place. The synthesis above is presented as general derivative-markets industry knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
